analysis.one_liner: Requires extra cost-benefit analysis, hearings, and court review before agencies can issue major federal regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee assignment: introduced in August 2015 and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, it received no markup, no debate, and no vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal rulemaking process for any regulation expected to cost the economy $100 million or more a year. Agencies would have to prove a rule's benefits justify its costs, adopt the least expensive option that meets the law's objectives, hold public hearings with cross-examination for the largest rules, and defend their choices in court under a tougher evidence standard. Supporters presented this as making regulators more accountable and transparent; the practical effect is that major public protections would take longer to issue and be easier to challenge or block.
analysis.who_benefits: Large companies that face expensive federal rules — on pollution, workplace safety, product safety, wages, and consumer finance — would gain new procedural tools to delay, narrow, or defeat those rules, and courts would be required to take the cheapest option unless the agency proves a costlier one is worth it.

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies, when writing any rule, to document the legal authority, the problem being addressed, alternatives considered, and — for major rules — a cost-benefit analysis.
Requires agencies to adopt the least costly rule considered that meets the statutory objectives, allowing a costlier rule only if the agency explains why the extra benefits justify the extra cost.

Gives any interested party the right to petition for a public hearing, with cross-examination of witnesses, on disputed factual issues in high-impact rules (those costing $1 billion or more a year), and the agency bears the burden of proof at such hearings.
Subjects high-impact rules and the denial of rulemaking petitions to judicial review under a 'substantial evidence' standard, making agency decisions easier to overturn in court.
Expands public participation: electronic dockets, longer comment periods (90 days for major rules), and a standing right to petition agencies to issue, amend, or repeal rules.

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on federal protections — cleaner air and water, safe workplaces, safe products, honest financial markets — would bear the cost as major rules are delayed for years, tied up in hearings and litigation, or watered down to the cheapest option available.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public relying on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The least-costly mandate would bar an agency from choosing a more protective rule — on toxic exposure, for example — unless it could prove in advance that the additional benefits justify the additional cost, a showing that is often difficult for health and safety rules.

Formal hearings with cross-examination on disputed science and economics would add months or years to rulemakings and give well-resourced companies a procedural stage that ordinary commenters cannot match.

The bill takes away court review of the government's own determination of whether a rule counts as a 'major rule,' so a misclassified rule could escape the tighter standards — or a rule could be swept into them — without judicial check.

Supporters' good-faith case is that agencies sometimes issue expensive rules on thin analysis and that dockets, longer comment periods, and hearings respond to legitimate complaints about opaque rulemaking; the transparency provisions have value independent of the cost mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces — public dockets, longer comment windows, documented reasoning — are real improvements available to anyone who reads them. But the bill's centerpiece is the least-costly-rule requirement plus a tougher court standard, and those fall hardest on exactly the rules with the largest stakes: protecting health, safety, and financial security. The costs would be diffuse and delayed, while the procedural advantages would flow to parties able to fund hearings, experts, and litigation. Weighed honestly, the bill trades broad, hard-to-see public costs for concentrated, measurable savings to regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rob Portman introduced the bill on August 6, 2015, joined by seven Republican colleagues and one Independent.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action — no committee markup, no floor debate, no vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their existing authority to issue major public protections without the added cost mandate, hearing requirements, and tougher court standard, and the people who depend on those protections were no worse off. Regulated industries gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public counting on federal protections

for.name: Rob Portman
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Regulatory Accountability Act of 2015 in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship included seven Republicans and one Independent (Angus King) with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill stalled in committee without recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Large regulated industries (energy, chemical, manufacturing, and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would have handed these companies procedural tools — hearings with cross-examination, a least-cost mandate, and easier court challenges — to delay or shrink the major rules that cost them the most. The savings to them would come from public protections arriving later or weaker.

industries.industry: Regulatory law firms and compliance shops
industries.note: Added hearings, expert testimony, petitions, and judicial review would create a larger market for the lawyers and consultants who work regulatory cases on behalf of companies facing new rules.
The bill would centralize review of major rules and guidance in OIRA, giving the administration's budget office more authority over what agencies may regulate and how they justify it.
